title: How to check your credit score and know which one lenders use
summary: Learn how to check your credit score easily and for free. Understand credit report factors impacting your score.

- How to check your credit score and know which one lenders use


Checking your credit score takes a few minutes and won’t lower it. The harder part is knowing which score you’re looking at, because a free app, your bank and a lender can each use a different scoring model and a different credit bureau’s data.


This guide covers the free ways to check, how to tell which score you’re seeing, which score lenders use, and how to fix errors on your report. If you’re buying a home, new to credit, or using an ITIN instead of a Social Security number, there’s a section for your situation too. Let’s start with the free options.


## Key takeaways


- You can check your credit score for free through your card issuer or bank, a free credit score site, a credit bureau or myFICO. Checking your own score doesn’t lower it.
- Free credit reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion are available every week at AnnualCreditReport.com, but a report usually doesn’t include your score.
- Every score comes from a scoring model, one bureau’s data and a date. When any of the three differ, two sources can show different numbers.
- Lenders use different scores for different loans. For mortgages sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, lenders can use Classic FICO or VantageScore 4.0.
- If you dispute an error, the bureau generally has 30 days to investigate, and up to 45 days if you send more information during that time.


## How to check your credit score for free


There are five common ways to see your score at no cost. Most of them tell you which scoring model and which bureau the number comes from, so make a note of both.


1. Check with your credit card issuer, bank or lender. Many major credit card companies and lenders show your score on your statement or online,[according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/where-can-i-get-my-credit-scores-en-316/) . Look for a credit score option in your account menu or app.
2. Use a free credit score site.[Credit Karma](https://www.creditkarma.com/free-credit-score) , for example, gives you free VantageScore 3.0 scores based on Equifax and TransUnion data. Read the fine print before you enter any payment information on any site.
3. Go to a credit bureau.[Experian offers a free FICO Score 8](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/how-do-you-check-your-credit-score/) based on its own data when you create a free account.[Equifax offers a free VantageScore 3.0 score](https://www.equifax.com/personal/products/credit/free-credit-score/) , updated daily, through an Equifax Core Credit account.
4. Sign up for the free plan on FICO’s own site,[myFICO](https://www.myfico.com/) . It includes a FICO Score 8 based on Equifax data.
5. Talk with a nonprofit counselor. Nonprofit credit counselors and housing counselors trained by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development can often give you a free credit report and score and help you review them, according to the CFPB.


FICO Score 8 is the most widely used version of the FICO score,[according to Credit Karma](https://www.creditkarma.com/credit/i/what-fico-score-8) . VantageScore 3.0 comes from a scoring company the three credit bureaus created in 2006.[VantageScore 3.0 scores](https://www.creditkarma.com/credit/i/vantagescore-30) run from 300 to 850, the same range as most FICO scores.


Your credit report is a separate check. You can get a free report from each of the three bureaus every week at AnnualCreditReport.com, the CFPB says. The report lists your accounts and payment history, but[in most cases it won’t include your credit score](https://www.usa.gov/credit-reports) .


## What does your credit score mean?


Most FICO and VantageScore credit scores use a 300-to-850 scale. Here’s how their scoring models break down:


[FICO](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/credit-scores)


**Exceptional credit:** 800-850


**Very good credit:** 740-799


**Good credit:** 670-739


**Fair credit:** 580-669


**Poor credit:** 300-579


[VantageScore](https://www.vantagescore.com/consumers/blog/the-complete-guide-to-your-vantagescore)


**Superprime credit:** 781-850


**Prime credit:** 661-780


**Near prime credit:** 601-660


**Subprime credit:** 300-600


You can have multiple versions of each credit score because not all credit bureaus and credit reporting entities use the same scoring systems.


For example, several websites and apps, like[Credit Karma](https://www.creditkarma.com/credit/i/credit-karma-app) , provide free scores. The scoring model of one bank, lender, or credit bureau may differ slightly from that of another. If you check your credit score through a couple of different entities, you’re likely to receive somewhat differing numbers. Credit Karma, for instance, labels the same VantageScore 3.0 ranges Excellent, Good, Fair and Poor. For what each range means in practice, see[what counts as a good credit score](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/good-credit-score/) .


## Which credit score are you seeing?


You don’t have just one credit score. You have several, and it’s normal for them to be slightly different, the CFPB notes. Three labels explain most of the gap between any two numbers:


- Scoring models such as FICO Score 8, VantageScore 3.0 and VantageScore 4.0 weigh the same information differently. Here’s more on[how a credit score works](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/what-is-credit-score/) .
- Equifax, Experian and TransUnion each keep their own report on you, and a lender may not report to all three.
- A score updated last month won’t reflect a balance you paid off last week.


Where you check Score model Bureau data


Experian free account FICO Score 8 Experian


Equifax Core Credit VantageScore 3.0 Equifax


Credit Karma VantageScore 3.0 Equifax and TransUnion


myFICO free plan FICO Score 8 Equifax


AnnualCreditReport.com No score Equifax, Experian and TransUnion reports


Before you compare two scores, run the three-label check: write down the model, the bureau and the date for each one. If any label differs, a gap is expected and doesn’t mean either source is wrong.


Say your banking app shows 712 and a free score site shows 690. If the first is a FICO Score 8 from Experian data and the second is a VantageScore 3.0 from TransUnion data, you’re looking at two different measures. Track each source against its own past readings, and look at your reports when one of them moves sharply.


## Which credit score will a lender use?


It depends on the lender and the loan. Lenders use different scores for different types of credit, so the score you check at home may not match the one on your application.


Mortgages are where the rules have moved most. Lenders that sell loans to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can now choose Classic FICO or VantageScore 4.0, and since September 9, 2026, any approved lender can use VantageScore 4.0,[according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency](https://www.fhfa.gov/policy/credit-scores) . FHFA calls this an interim policy, and for now those lenders still pull reports from all three bureaus.


For other credit,[FICO says](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/fico-scores-bridge) “90% of top lenders use FICO® Scores,” though a lender can choose which version to pull. If a lender denies your application or takes another unfavorable action based on your credit report, you can get a free copy of that report from the bureau named in the notice if you ask within 60 days,[per the Federal Trade Commission](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/free-credit-reports) .


Your personal score can matter for a business, too. Shanna Watkins, co-founder of the nonalcoholic beverage brand Sensori, described how that played out for her on the Mind the Business podcast:


> “I had taken care of my credit for you know, years and years and built that up to where I had a really good credit score. So I was like, Okay, I’m gonna go and I’m gonna get a line of credit that could just be that initial capital to get us started.”
>
>
> Shanna Watkins, co-founder of Sensori, on[Resilience and Reinvention](https://omny.fm/shows/mind-the-business-small-business-success-stories/resilience-and-reinvention)


## Should you pay for your credit score?


Most people don’t need to. Paying makes the most sense when you want a specific version a lender uses. myFICO’s paid plans, for example, include FICO Score 2 and FICO Score 4, which myFICO says are used by mortgage lenders.


Watch for free trials. A free trial might last only for a set period, after which you must cancel or pay a monthly fee, the CFPB warns. If you do buy a score, you don’t have to buy any other services offered with it.


## How often can you check your credit score without hurting it?


There’s no need to limit how often you check your credit score. Checking your own credit is considered a soft inquiry, not a hard inquiry. Soft inquiries don’t[impact your credit score](https://www.equifax.com/personal/education/credit/score/articles/-/learn/will-checking-your-credit-hurt-credit-scores/) , so regularly checking your score won’t hurt it.


A hard inquiry happens when you apply for credit and a lender checks your report. It can stay on your report for up to two years,[per Credit Karma](https://www.creditkarma.com/credit/i/hard-credit-inquiries-and-soft-credit-inquiries) . For most people, one more inquiry takes less than five points off their FICO Scores,[according to FICO](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/credit-reports/credit-checks-and-inquiries) .


You’ll also want to review your credit report periodically, which lists your payment history, open lines of credit, and outstanding debt. Since free reports are available weekly, checking each bureau’s report a few times a year costs nothing.


Reviewing your report can help spot cases of fraud or outstanding debt or credit you’ve forgotten about. A credit report is a type of credit reference required when borrowing money from a service or lender. So, if you’re planning on buying a house and will need a loan, look at your credit report to ensure you’re in good standing.


## How to check your credit score in your situation


The right steps depend on why you’re checking and how much credit history you have.


### If you’re buying a home


Pull all three credit reports a few months before you apply, since mortgage lenders sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac check all three bureaus. That gives you time to dispute errors before a lender sees them. Expect the score on your mortgage application to differ from the one in a free app.


### If you’re new to credit


You can have a credit report and still have no score. A FICO score generally needs an account that has been open and reported for six months, while VantageScore can score you sooner,[according to Credit Karma](https://www.creditkarma.com/credit/i/vantagescore-vs-fico) . Say you opened your first secured card in March. A VantageScore-based app may show a score by summer, before a FICO-based tool does. These steps to[build credit from scratch](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/build-credit/) can help you get there.


### If you have an ITIN instead of a Social Security number


You can have a credit report and score without a Social Security number,[Experian says](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/can-you-check-your-credit-score-without-a-social-security-number/) . Experian’s guidance notes that AnnualCreditReport.com asks for a Social Security number, and that you can request your Experian report in writing instead, with a copy of a government-issued ID and a recent utility bill or bank statement. Check the current steps before you mail anything. Ask Equifax and TransUnion directly how to request yours.


## Steps to take if you find errors in your credit report


If you’re in the process of repairing your credit, it’s important to maintain a clean and accurate credit report. To do that, you should monitor your report regularly and fix any errors that appear. Fixing any errors in your report requires these eight steps:


1. Get your free reports from all three bureaus at AnnualCreditReport.com.[Credit Karma](https://www.creditkarma.com/lp/free-credit-scores-v12a) also shows your Equifax and TransUnion reports.
2. Review reports carefully for anything that looks suspicious or inaccurate.
3. Gather supporting documents proving these errors.
4. File disputes with relevant credit bureaus online, by mail, or by phone.
5. Contact the information provider (e.g., bank or credit card company) about the error.
6. Wait for the investigation results (typically 30 days, or[up to 45 days](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681i) if you send more information during the investigation).
7. Review the outcome. The bureau must send you the results in writing, along with a copy of your report that reflects them.
8. If unresolved, consider adding a statement of dispute, filing a[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) complaint](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/complaint/) , or seeking legal advice.


## Understanding identity and credit fraud


Pulling your credit score won’t give you direct information regarding fraudulent activity, but it could be a clue that fraudulent activity has occurred. If your credit score looks suspicious, pull your credit report or sign up for credit monitoring.


## Check your credit score with Credit Karma


Intuit Credit Karma gives you free VantageScore 3.0 scores and reports from Equifax and TransUnion and lets you know when your scores change.[Create a free Credit Karma account](https://www.creditkarma.com/signup) to start tracking yours, and use the three-label check whenever you compare it with another score.


If you want to learn more about your personal finances overall and how your credit score fits in, check out Intuit for Education, our[free financial literacy curriculum](https://www.intuit.com/solutions/education/learners/) . Its goal is to help you gain confidence in your own personal finances.


## Frequently asked questions about checking your credit score


### Does checking your credit score lower it?


No. Checking your own credit is a soft inquiry, which doesn’t affect your score. A hard inquiry happens when you apply for credit and a lender checks your report.


### Why is my credit score different on different sites?


Each score comes from a scoring model, one bureau’s data and a date. If any of those differ, two sources can show different numbers, and that’s normal.


### How often can I get my credit report for free?


Every week. You can get a free report from each of the three credit bureaus at AnnualCreditReport.com, though a report usually doesn’t include your score.
